source.title: Concept Evolution in Deep Learning Training: A Unified Interpretation Framework and Discoveries
source.authors: Haekyu Park; Seongmin Lee; Benjamin Hoover; Austin P. Wright; Omar Shaikh; Rahul Duggal; Nilaksh Das; Kevin Li; Judy Hoffman; Duen Horng Chau

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses neurons as units for interpreting concept evolution and reports evaluations of its own framework, but does not test the claim's neuron-pole job shares or the other listed versions.
record.gate_note: The paper explicitly allows many-to-many neuron-concept relationships, including polysemantic neurons, but does not quantify how many neuron poles have one or more jobs. Its human-evaluation AUC results assess whether participants agree with ConceptEvo's neuron groupings, not the share of interpretable neurons or prediction of activations on held-out examples. Results about concept diversity, evolution importance and training dynamics do not measure the behaviors named in the claim versions.
record.test_reason: ConceptEvo uses vision-model neurons as concept units and evaluates its own embedding and grouping method (human intruder-task AUC, accuracy drop on reverting evolutions). It reports no share of neurons with one job, no InceptionV1 cat-car analysis, no tool or architecture effect on interpretable share, no circuit graphs, and no held-out activation prediction.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct in substance. The authors conclude ConceptEvo aligns concepts across models and epochs in a way humans find meaningful. They also find the discovered evolutions important for class predictions, and that the framework helps diagnose training problems such as lost concept diversity and slow evolution under overfitting.
record.recipe_differences: The paper proposes ConceptEvo for tracking visual-neuron concept evolution during training; it does not reproduce the neuron-pole audit or test the listed claim versions.

fits_no_version.finding: Human raters distinguished ConceptEvo neuron groups from intruders with AUC 0.86–0.90, versus 0.98 for hand-picked groups.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neuron groupings from a co-activation embedding are judged semantically coherent by humans across models and training epochs.

fits_no_version.finding: In VGG16 and ConvNeXt trained with overly high learning rates, almost all (VGG16) and over 30% (ConvNeXt) of last-conv-layer neurons respond predominantly to backgrounds.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Poor training hyperparameters collapse neuron concept diversity in late layers.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 32nd ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM ’23)
record.problems: The human-evaluation AUC results do not measure the proportion of interpretable neurons or test explanations on held-out activations. Uncertainty for the reported AUC values is not stated.

untested.parts: All: shares across language models and scale.
All: InceptionV1 cat-car neuron, pose, recursive generalization.
All: interpretable share as a function of tools and architecture. The ConvNeXt vs VGG comparison concerns concept evolution, not interpretable share.
All: neuron-based attribution graphs and replacement models.
All: whether activating-example explanations predict firing elsewhere.

record.verdict_notes: The paper only acknowledges polysemantic neurons as part of its embedding design and never quantifies them. All rows are method-evaluation results; it is correctly classed T4 with no verdicts.

versions.untested_parts: The one-job, two-related-jobs and not-understood shares for Qwen3-32B.
Shares across language models, dense and mixture-of-experts models, and parameter scales.
The InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose detection and recursive generalization.
The proportion of interpretable neurons as a function of tools, architecture or capacity, including the InceptionV1-sized model estimates.
Attribution graphs, behavioral explanations, replacement models and reconstruction error.
Whether explanations from activating examples predict where neurons fire on other examples.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.
